title: Tenant Rights in India: What You Actually Have, and What You Don’t
seoTitle: Tenant Rights in India: What You Actually Have
description: Tenancy is a state subject, so tenant rights in India vary. What the Model Tenancy Act proposes, what protects you now, and what to do when it goes wrong.
excerpt: There is no single national tenancy law in India, and the Model Tenancy Act binds nobody until a state enacts it. Here is what actually protects you, and what to do when a landlord ignores it.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: Renters who have read their own agreements the hard way

faq.q: Is the Model Tenancy Act, 2021 the law in my state?
faq.a: Only if your state has enacted it, or its own tenancy legislation based on it. The Model Tenancy Act was approved by the Union Cabinet in June 2021 as a template for states to adopt, adapt or ignore — rental housing is a state subject, so the centre cannot impose it. A few states have passed their own tenancy laws and more are at various stages. Check your state housing department before assuming its protections apply to you.

faq.q: Can my landlord enter the flat without telling me?
faq.a: Renting a home means taking possession of it for a term, so a landlord letting themselves in while you are out disturbs the very thing you are paying for. Whether you can enforce that depends on your agreement and your state’s law — the Model Tenancy Act proposes advance written notice, but that binds only where enacted. The practical fix is a one-line entry clause in the agreement before you sign, plus a written message on the record the first time it happens.

faq.q: Can a landlord change the locks or cut off water and electricity to make me leave?
faq.a: No. Lawful eviction runs through a legal process, not through the front door. Indian law protects settled possession, and someone dispossessed by force can go to court to recover it even against the owner. Cutting off essential services to make staying unbearable is treated as coercion rather than a utilities matter, and a lockout or threats can be a police issue, not just a civil one.

faq.q: Can my landlord increase the rent in the middle of the agreement?
faq.a: Generally not unilaterally. A tenancy agreement fixes the rent for its term, so a mid-term increase is a request you can decline, with renewal becoming the real negotiation. Where a state has enacted a tenancy law, revision usually has a defined notice route and a forum to object. Check your escalation clause — and be wary of one that says "as mutually agreed" rather than a stated figure.

faq.q: Who pays for repairs — the landlord or the tenant?
faq.a: The usual split is structure to the owner and daily wear to the tenant: seepage, wiring, plumbing behind walls and structural cracks are the landlord’s; bulbs, blocked drains and damage you caused are yours. The disputes live in the middle, which is why a rupee threshold written into the agreement is worth insisting on. Report everything in writing, and never repair a landlord’s item on the assumption you will be reimbursed.

faq.q: Is it legal for a landlord to refuse me because I am single, a bachelor, or because of my food habits or religion?
faq.a: The honest answer is that India has no general statute prohibiting a private landlord from choosing a tenant on these grounds, and constitutional equality guarantees operate mainly against the State rather than private owners. Some society rules and refusals have been criticised and challenged, and other laws can apply in specific contexts such as caste-based exclusion, but there is no quick, reliable remedy. Practically, ask before you visit, deal with owners rather than intermediaries, and look at independent buildings where a committee cannot overrule the owner.

body:
The first time Meera's landlord let himself into her flat, she was at work.

She found out from a WhatsApp message that afternoon — a photograph of her own kitchen, and a short note about the state of the sink. He'd come to check a leak, he said. He had a key. It was his flat.

She sat with that for a day. Then she did what everyone does: searched "tenant rights India" between meetings and got back a list of very confident sentences. Deposits capped at two months. Twenty-four hours' notice before entry. No eviction without a court order.

Almost none of it matched her agreement. Some didn't apply where she lived at all. And when she asked a lawyer friend, she got the least satisfying answer available: *it depends which state you're in.*

That's the honest starting point for this whole subject. Better to get used to it early than to discover it mid-argument.

## Why there's no single answer to "what are my rights?"

Most countries have one tenancy law. India doesn't, and the reason is constitutional rather than accidental.

Land, and the relationship between landlord and tenant, is a **State subject**. Each state legislates for itself. That's why renters in Chennai, Lucknow and Bengaluru can be living under genuinely different rules while paying rent into the same banking system.

For decades most states ran on rent control statutes drafted for a very different economy — written when the anxiety was runaway rents in a housing shortage, and whose main effect over time was to make owners reluctant to let property out at all. Many of those old Acts are still on the books. Some apply only to older buildings, or below a certain rent, or in notified areas. Whether one applies to you has a real answer, but it's a state-by-state, sometimes city-by-city answer.

Sitting above all of that is central law — the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 sets out default rights and duties between a lessor and a lessee. But those defaults apply *in the absence of a contract to the contrary*, and they yield to state rent legislation. Which brings you to the practical truth:

> For most urban renters in India today, the document that determines your rights is not a statute. It's the agreement you signed.

That's why the [rental agreement deserves far more attention than people give it](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india). It isn't paperwork. It's the operating rules of your home for the next eleven months.

## The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 — a good law that binds almost nobody

In June 2021 the Union Cabinet approved the **Model Tenancy Act, 2021**. If you've read anything reassuring about Indian tenant rights in the last few years, it was probably describing this.

It's a sensible document. Among other things it proposes:

- A **Rent Authority** to register tenancy agreements and handle routine disputes, with a **Rent Court** and **Rent Tribunal** above it — so tenancy disputes don't queue behind everything else in ordinary civil courts
- A cap on security deposits: two months' rent for residential premises, six for non-residential
- Refund of the deposit at the time the tenant hands back the premises
- **Advance written notice before the landlord enters** (the model text asks for twenty-four hours)
- A structure for repairs, essential services and rent revision in writing rather than by argument

Now the caveat that changes everything, and the most misreported fact about renting in India: **a model law is a template, not a law.** The centre circulated it so states could adopt it, adapt it, or leave it alone. Until your state passes its own tenancy legislation, that two-month cap protects you precisely as much as a good idea in a PDF protects anyone.

A handful of states have enacted their own tenancy laws — Tamil Nadu's came in 2017, before the model was even published, and requires agreements to be registered with a rent authority. Others have moved since. The list genuinely changes.

So the useful habit isn't memorising the Model Tenancy Act. It's this: **find out what your own state has actually enacted, and whether it covers your tenancy.** Ask a local lawyer, check your state housing department's site, or ask the rent authority if one exists. Ten minutes of that beats any article, including this one.

## Peaceful enjoyment: the flat is yours while you're paying for it

Here is something that holds up well across jurisdictions and is easy to state plainly.

When you rent a home you aren't buying permission to be a guest in someone else's property. You're taking possession of it for a term. The landlord owns it; for the duration, you *occupy* it. That's the whole basis of what lawyers call quiet or peaceful enjoyment — having handed you possession, the landlord doesn't get to disturb it at will.

So a landlord letting himself in while you're at work is not merely rude. It's a breach of the thing you're paying for.

But — and this is where Meera got stuck — enforcing it depends on what your agreement says and what your state's law provides. If the agreement is silent, you're arguing from general principle rather than from a clause. So the fix is upstream, not downstream:

**Put entry in writing before you sign.** One sentence is enough. Something like: *the landlord may enter only with the tenant's prior consent, on reasonable advance notice, except in a genuine emergency such as fire or a burst pipe.* Most owners agree without a second thought, because it's obviously reasonable. The ones who bristle at it have told you something useful for free.

Same with keys. It's normal for an owner to keep a spare. It is not normal for them to use it while you're out. Say so warmly at the start, not angrily six months in.

If it happens anyway: message them. Not a call. A message, so it exists. Factual, unemotional — *you came into the flat today while I was out; please give me notice and let me be there in future.* You're not picking a fight. You're creating a record, and records are the only thing that survives a disagreement.

## Eviction is a process, not a padlock

Here the gap between belief and truth is widest, in both directions.

Tenants often assume they can't be removed. They can — for non-payment, for breach of the agreement, at the end of the term, on grounds that vary by state. Landlords often assume that because they own the place, they can end the arrangement whenever they like, by whatever means. They can't.

Hold on to the shape rather than the detail: **lawful eviction runs through a legal process, not through the front door.** Indian law has long protected settled possession — a person in occupation can't simply be dispossessed by force, and someone thrown out that way can go to court to recover possession, even against the owner.

What that rules out:

- **Changing the locks** while you're at work, or padlocking the gate
- **Cutting off water or electricity** to make staying unbearable
- Removing a door, a fitting, or your belongings
- Threats, or bringing people around to intimidate you into leaving

Disconnecting essential services to force someone out is coercion dressed as a utilities issue, and it's treated as unlawful whatever your state's tenancy position. Physical dispossession or threats can be a police matter, not just a civil one.

What I won't give you is a notice period. Notice requirements, permitted grounds and the process are state-specific and agreement-specific, and anyone telling you "your landlord must give you X months" as a national rule is guessing. Read your termination clause. Then check your state.

The honest asymmetry: even where the law is clearly on your side, enforcing it takes time you don't have if you're locked out on a Tuesday.

## Rent increases in the middle of a term

You signed for eleven months at ₹32,000. In month five a message arrives: rent goes up to ₹36,000 from next month.

Can they do that? Generally no — not unilaterally, not mid-term. A tenancy agreement fixes the rent for its term. A landlord who wants more can ask, you can say no, and the realistic consequence is that renewal becomes a negotiation. What they can't ordinarily do is rewrite an agreed figure halfway through because the market moved.

Where states have enacted tenancy laws, revision usually has a defined route — written notice, a period, a forum to object. Where they haven't, your agreement is the answer again. So look for two things when you sign:

1. **The escalation clause.** Many agreements build in a percentage increase on renewal. That's normal. What matters is that it's a stated number, not "as mutually agreed" — which means "as the landlord decides once you're settled in and moving is expensive".
2. **A clause saying rent won't change during the term.** Obvious, frequently absent.

If a mid-term increase is demanded anyway, reply in writing, politely, citing the clause. Most of these attempts are opportunistic rather than determined, and they don't survive a calm reply that shows you've read the agreement.

## Repairs and essential services: who owes what

The default understanding, which most agreements track: the **structure** is the owner's problem, the **wear of daily use** is the tenant's.

Leaking roof, plumbing behind a wall, seepage, wiring, a geyser that dies of old age, structural cracks: landlord. Fused bulb, the drain you clogged, damage you caused, a tap washer: tenant.

The trouble is the middle. Who pays when the five-year-old washing machine that came with the flat stops working? When the borewell pump fails?

Three habits make it manageable:

- **Get the split written down.** Many agreements set a rupee threshold — under it the tenant's, above it the landlord's. That's a fair mechanism when the number is sensible.
- **Report in writing, always.** A thread showing you reported seepage in March is worth a lot in November, both for getting it fixed and for the deposit conversation later.
- **Never fix a landlord's item assuming you'll be reimbursed.** Agree the cost first, in writing. Otherwise you've made a gift.

And be clear about what's a charge rather than a repair. Maintenance, water and society charges are recurring costs that belong in the agreement as numbers — a big part of the [gap between advertised rent and what you actually pay](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india).

## The part with no clean legal answer: discrimination

Let's not be coy, because pretending otherwise helps nobody.

If you're a bachelor, a group of young men, unmarried, a woman living alone, from a particular religion, or someone who eats meat, you have very likely been refused a flat for that reason in an Indian city. Often politely. Sometimes in the listing itself. Occasionally by a housing society rather than the owner.

The honest legal position: India's constitutional equality guarantees operate mainly against the State. There is no general national statute stopping a private landlord from choosing a tenant on these grounds the way housing discrimination law works in some other countries. Some society rules and refusals have been challenged and criticised, including by courts, and other laws can bite in specific contexts such as caste-based exclusion. But a broad, quick, reliable remedy for "he wouldn't rent to me because I'm single" does not exist.

I'd rather say that plainly than dress up a route that costs you months and probably doesn't get you the flat.

What actually helps:

- **Ask before you visit**, not after you've spent a Sunday travelling. The question saves more than it costs.
- **Deal with owners, not intermediaries.** Brokers frequently apply filters the owner never asked for, because it's easier for them.
- **Bring the paperwork that removes the stated excuse.** Employment letter, ID, previous landlord reference, bank statement. It doesn't touch prejudice, but it dissolves the "we prefer families, it's about reliability" version surprisingly often.
- **Independent buildings over societies** if you keep hitting society rules. The owner can say yes without a committee.
- **Keep a record** if a refusal comes in writing, especially from a society. It costs nothing to save a screenshot.

None of that is justice. It's the workaround people actually use, and it beats being blindsided at the door.

## What to actually do when something goes wrong

An escalation ladder, cheapest first. Don't skip steps — each one strengthens the next.

1. **Move the conversation to writing.** Whatever was said on the phone, follow it up: *just to confirm — you'll fix the seepage by the 15th.* Not adversarial. You're making the conversation exist.
2. **Send a clear, dated written request.** Email if you have one; WhatsApp is imperfect but real. State the facts, the clause, what you want, by when. Short and unemotional — angry messages get quoted back at you, boring ones don't.
3. **Send a formal legal notice.** Through a lawyer, on letterhead, by registered post. It costs relatively little, and a surprising number of disputes end here because it signals you'll go further.
4. **Approach the Rent Authority or Rent Court**, if your state has enacted a tenancy law establishing one. Where they exist, they're the right forum.
5. **Otherwise, civil court or consumer forum.** Slow. Sometimes worth it for large sums, often not for small ones. Get an opinion on the arithmetic first.
6. **Police only for genuine coercion** — a lockout, a threat, intimidation, forced entry, belongings removed. A rent dispute is civil and the police will rightly say so. Being locked out of your home is not.

Two things about this ladder. It works better the earlier you're on it — the record built in step one is what makes steps three and four viable. And **remedies in India are slow**: a dispute that's morally clear can still take a long time. Which leads to the sentence this article is really about.

> Documentation before the problem is worth more than rights after it.

## Common mistakes

**Assuming a law applies to you because you read about it.** The Model Tenancy Act is the biggest trap. Verify your own state.

**Treating the agreement as a formality.** It's the primary source of your rights. Read every clause, including the boring ones about entry, repairs, notice and renewal. A short [list of questions asked before you sign](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting) prevents most of what this article is about.

**Handling everything by phone.** A call is not a record. If it matters, message afterwards to summarise it.

**Not confirming who actually owns the flat.** People pay deposits to someone with no authority to let the property more often than you'd think — a recurring pattern in [rental fraud](/blog/rental-scams-in-india). Ask for the title document or tax receipt, and meet the owner once.

**Escalating to anger instead of to paper.** Shouting feels better and achieves less. The boring, documented person usually wins.

**Adjusting rent against the deposit to "settle" a dispute.** It feels efficient and destroys your position. Keep them separate — the [mechanics of getting a deposit back](/blog/security-deposits-in-india) are their own subject.

**Leaving without a written handover.** Date, meter readings, keys returned, in a message. Otherwise the timeline becomes a matter of memory.

## What experience teaches

**Photograph the flat on the day you get the keys.** Empty rooms, every defect, close up. Ninety minutes that settles arguments about damage, repairs and deposits at once. It's the highest-return habit in Indian renting and belongs at the top of any [move-in routine](/blog/house-hunting-checklist-india).

**Ask the outgoing tenant one question.** Not "was it nice" — ask whether the landlord was reasonable about repairs, and how the deposit went. Nothing you can inspect tells you as much.

**Be an easy tenant about everything except records.** Pay on time, don't create drama, fix small things yourself, and be quietly rigorous about writing things down. That combination is what gets you a landlord who returns your calls in month nine.

**Keep one folder**, backed up: agreement, ID copies, payment receipts, repair messages, move-in photos. If you ever need it, you'll need all of it at once.

**Know your building's people** — the watchman, the secretary, the neighbour on your floor. In a lockout, a witness who saw it is worth more than any clause.

## Where StayOnMap helps, and where it can't

Straightforwardly: a rental platform claiming to protect your legal rights would be selling you something it can't deliver.

We can't enforce anyone's rights. We don't hold your money, we aren't a party to your agreement, and if a landlord behaves badly the remedies above are the ones that exist.

What we can do is remove some fog before you commit. Every listing states the rent, the deposit and the maintenance as required fields, so the numbers you'll be negotiating around are visible before you visit rather than revealed in a stairwell. There's no brokerage. And you contact the owner directly rather than through an intermediary — which matters more than it sounds here, because the person answering your questions about entry, repairs and notice is the person who'll be on the other end of them.

That's the whole claim: better information earlier, fewer people in between.

## What to remember

There is no single national tenancy law in India, and there may not be one for a long time. Tenancy is a state subject, many states still run on old rent control statutes, and the Model Tenancy Act, 2021 — genuinely sensible — binds nobody until a state enacts it. Find out where your state stands, rather than taking any article's word for it, this one included.

Your agreement is doing most of the work. Entry, repairs, notice, renewal, rent revision — get them written down before you sign, when you still have leverage, rather than argued afterwards when you don't.

And when something goes wrong: writing first, legal notice second, Rent Authority where it exists, police only for genuine coercion. Expect it to be slower than it should be.

Meera didn't sue anybody. She sent one calm message that evening saying she'd like notice before he came in, and she added a line about entry to the agreement at renewal. He grumbled and signed it.

Two years later he still has a key. He's never used it without asking.
